Fe3O4/carbon composite nanofibers were prepared by electrospinning PAN/AAI/DMF solution followed by stabilization at 260°C and carbonization at 500–800°C.
SEM and TEM images show uniform fibers with well-dispersed Fe3O4 nanoparticles inside or on the fiber surface.
XRD confirms the presence of Fe3O4 nanoparticles with an average size of ~50 nm in fibers carbonized at 700°C.
Electrical conductivity of composite fibers increases with AAI content up to 2 wt%, reaching 90–120 S/m depending on carbonization temperature.
Magnetic hysteresis loops indicate that saturation magnetization (Ms) increases with AAI content, e.g., Ms = 13.53 emu/g for 3 wt% AAI at 800°C.
Permittivity (ε') and dielectric loss (ε'') decrease with frequency but are higher in composites with Fe3O4 than in pure carbon fibers.
Fiber/paraffin composite samples with 5 wt.% fiber ratio show optimal microwave absorption performance.
Reflection loss (RL) reaches minimum values between −40 and −45 dB at 5 mm coating thickness and 5 wt.% fiber ratio.
Absorption bandwidth under −5 dB reflection loss can reach 12–13 GHz in the 2–18 GHz frequency range.
Increasing AAI content beyond 2 wt% can hinder graphitization and reduce absorption performance.
Microwave absorption mechanisms include dielectric loss from dipolar and interfacial polarization, magnetic loss from Fe3O4 nanoparticles, and defect-induced polarization.
Dielectric loss tangent (tan δe) values for composites range from 0.5 to 1, significantly higher than pure carbon fibers (~0.2).
Coating thickness influences absorption peak frequency and bandwidth, with thicker coatings improving performance.
Fe3O4 nanoparticles catalyze graphitization, improving electrical conductivity and microwave absorption.
Composite nanofibers outperform pure carbon nanofibers in low-frequency (2–5 GHz) absorption, addressing a common weakness in microwave absorbers.
The composite materials exhibit good impedance matching with free space, enhancing microwave entry and attenuation.
The study uses Transmission Line Theory and vector network analyzer data to calculate reflection loss.
The fiber diameters decrease from 300–400 nm (as-spun) to 200–300 nm after carbonization.
Magnetic properties arise due to Fe3O4 nanoparticles embedded in the carbon matrix.
The optimal carbonization temperature for microwave absorption is around 700–800°C.
Paraffin is used as a matrix material with low permittivity and permeability to isolate the effect of nanofibers.
